summary: Specifies the EAP key hierarchy and a framework for transporting and using key material generated by EAP methods. It includes a system-level security analysis and checks conditions for meeting the guidelines in RFC 4962. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Passing a secret key through many hands needs rules. This paper explains the family tree of keys and how they are used safely.

subtitle: How the keys made by EAP login methods are named, scoped, handed to the network and kept safe.

tldr.problem: EAP lets a device and a server authenticate each other and derive keys, but EAP itself does not say how those keys are named, carried to the network device, used by the lower layer, or kept from leaking.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the EAP key hierarchy (MSK, EMSK and related parameters), a three-phase conversation, four invariants that keep EAP independent of mode, media, method and ciphersuite, and rules for how lower layers and AAA protocols may use the keys.
tldr.outcome: It also gives a system-level security analysis against the requirements of RFC 4962. It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3748 and has itself been updated by RFC 8940.

today: RFC 5247 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3748 and has been updated by RFC 8940, so read it together with that update.

sections.title: What the Framework Covers
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP, RFC 3748) enables extensible network access authentication. It was developed for use with PPP, and has since been applied to IEEE 802 wired networks, IKEv2 and wireless networks such as IEEE 802.11 and IEEE 802.16e.

EAP is a two-party protocol spoken between the EAP peer and the EAP server. Its authentication algorithms, called methods, generate keying material. Part of it is used by the methods themselves, and part is exported. Methods can also export parameters such as the authenticated peer and server identities and a unique conversation identifier, and can import and export lower-layer parameters called channel bindings.

This RFC specifies the EAP key hierarchy and a framework for transporting and using that material. It also gives a detailed security analysis of the conditions under which the key management guidelines of RFC 4962 can be satisfied.
sections.eli5: When you prove who you are to a network, a secret key is made along the way. This paper is the rulebook for who may hold that key and what they may do with it.

sections.title: The Three-Phase Conversation
sections.content:
Where EAP key derivation is supported, the conversation typically has three phases:

  • Phase 0, Discovery: peers locate authenticators and learn their capabilities.
  • Phase 1, Authentication: phase 1a is the EAP authentication itself, where keying material is derived on the peer and the EAP server. Phase 1b is the optional AAA key transport, which carries the keying material from a backend authentication server to the authenticator.
  • Phase 2, Secure Association Protocol: the peer and authenticator create unicast (2a) and optionally multicast (2b) security associations.

Phases 0, 1b and 2 are handled outside EAP. The lower-layer protocol handles phases 0 and 2, and a AAA protocol such as RADIUS or Diameter typically handles phase 1b.

Finishing EAP does not by itself commit the peer to joining the network. That commitment is implied by creating a security association between the peer and the authenticator in phase 2. The RFC gives examples of how existing lower layers handle these phases: PPP has neither discovery nor a Secure Association Protocol, IEEE 802.11 discovers access points with Beacon and Probe frames and uses its 4-way handshake for phase 2, and IKEv2 handles unicast associations but typically needs a separate group key protocol for multicast.
sections.eli5: First you find the door, then you show your ID to the guard, and finally you and the doorkeeper agree on a private handshake. Only the last step makes you a member.

sections.title: The EAP Key Hierarchy
sections.content:
At the root is the long-term credential of the chosen method, such as a pre-shared key or the private key matching a certificate. From it, methods derive two kinds of keying material. Local material, such as the Transient EAP Keys (TEKs), is used inside the method and not exported. Exported material is the Master Session Key (MSK), the Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) and an optional Initialization Vector (IV).

A method supporting key derivation MUST export an MSK and an EMSK of at least 64 octets each. The IV is deprecated, because in methods such as EAP-TLS it is a known value, and it is optional for methods to generate it. The EMSK MUST NOT be provided to any entity outside the EAP server or peer, and nothing from which it could be computed may be passed out either.

Methods that derive keys and authenticate both sides SHOULD also export a Session-Id that uniquely identifies the conversation, one or more Peer-Ids, and optionally Server-Ids. Methods written after this RFC MUST define all three. The Session-Id is the EAP Type Code joined with a Method-Id, or for expanded types 0xFE followed by the Vendor-Id, the Vendor-Type and the Method-Id. Every key has a name and a scope, and the MSK and EMSK MUST be named using the Session-Id plus an indication of which material is meant. Appendix A lists how existing methods define these parameters.
sections.eli5: There is one big secret, like a master recipe. From it the login method cooks a few dishes: some stay in the kitchen and some go out to the lower layer. Every dish gets a name tag so nobody mixes them up.

sections.title: The Four EAP Invariants
sections.content:
The RFC names four basic properties that hold for EAP implementations.

  • Mode independence: an authenticator can run methods locally or act as a pass-through to a backend authentication server. EAP methods behave identically either way, including key derivation and parameter import and export. The main job of the AAA protocol within EAP is to preserve this.
  • Media independence: methods work on any lower layer that meets the criteria in RFC 3748. They cannot assume knowledge of the lower layer and treat channel binding parameters as opaque octets.
  • Method independence: a pass-through authenticator need not implement any method, so it cannot be assumed to support any method-specific code.
  • Ciphersuite independence: the ciphersuite protecting data after authentication is negotiated between peer and authenticator in the lower layer, so methods export keying material that works for any ciphersuite. Algorithms for deriving TSKs MUST NOT depend on the EAP method, although TEK derivation MAY be method-specific.

Ciphersuite independence means methods need no update when a new ciphersuite appears, stay simpler, and avoid ciphersuite-specific configuration.
sections.eli5: The login method should not care how the network is wired, who runs the front desk, or what lock is on the door. That way each part can change without breaking the others.

sections.title: How Lower Layers Use the Keys
sections.content:
When EAP finishes, the exported material and parameters go to the lower layer and the AAA layer. The rules are strict. Lower layers MUST NOT export keys passed down by EAP methods, and the material MUST NOT be used in another lower layer or transported to another entity. On the server, material may be replicated to the authenticator's AAA layer, except for the EMSK. The EAP layer, peer and authenticator layers MUST NOT modify or cache material passing between the method and the lower layer.

Lower layers MAY cache keying material only where they explicitly support it, and new lower-layer specifications MUST describe their caching behavior. A AAA layer that has sent keys MUST delete them and MUST NOT retain them. Section 2.1 compares existing lower layers, as the table below summarizes.

The RFC also asks that authenticators and peers be identified explicitly, not by endpoint addresses, because either side may have several ports and one physical authenticator may present several virtual ones. It recommends the NAS-Identifier attribute for naming the authenticator. If virtual authenticators share a key cache, a peer could use keys from a Guest network to reach a Corporate Intranet network. The RFC therefore requires authenticators to cache the associated authorizations with the keys, and recommends separate key caches per virtual authenticator.
sections.eli5: A key handed to one door's lock must stay with that door. It may not be copied, shared with another door, or carried off. After the key has been delivered, the courier must throw their copy away.

sections.title: Security Association Management
sections.content:
EAP supports key derivation but not the management of lower-layer security associations. It does not negotiate those associations, re-key exported material without re-authentication, synchronize key installation and deletion, negotiate lifetimes, or guarantee that session keys are fresh. A post-EAP handshake called the Secure Association Protocol is meant to fill these gaps.

The RFC recommends it provide entity naming, mutual proof of possession of the keying material, secure capabilities negotiation, key naming, fresh Transient Session Keys (TSKs), key lifetime management and resynchronization. Where a lower layer caches keying material, this phase is REQUIRED and MUST derive fresh unicast and multicast TSKs even when the transported material is not fresh, typically by mixing in nonces or counters. It MUST operate directly between the peer and authenticator and MUST NOT be passed through to the backend server.

A child key may live no longer than its parent: derived keys can last as long as the MSK and EMSK or less, but not longer. Where no lifetime can be learned, a default lifetime of 8 hours is RECOMMENDED. The RFC advises against managing lifetimes inside EAP methods. It notes that the key wrap used by RADIUS has known problems, and that RADIUS over IPsec is the recommended approach.
sections.eli5: EAP hands over the key but does not say when to change the locks or how to prove who has which key. A second handshake on top does that, and it makes a brand new working key every time, even if the main key is reused.

sections.title: Handoff Vulnerabilities
sections.content:
A handoff happens when a peer moves to a new authenticator. Several schemes aim to cut handoff delay: EAP pre-authentication, proactive key distribution, key caching, context transfer and token distribution. Each skips or shortens some phases. For example, pre-authentication only moves EAP authentication off the critical path, while key caching avoids phases 1a and 1b but still needs discovery and the Secure Association Protocol.

Skipping the AAA exchange raises authorization problems. For a handoff to be correct, it MUST establish on the new authenticator the same authorizations as a full AAA conversation would have. Problems include theft of service, loss of network-wide state such as concurrent session counts, and elevation of privilege. An example is a user with guest VLAN access being given unrestricted access when the new authenticator has different VLAN capabilities.

The RFC says that if a successful handoff would produce incorrect authorizations, it is preferable for it to fail. Proactive key distribution also depends on the server's knowledge of the "neighbor graph", and a compromised authenticator could corrupt it with forged identification attributes.
sections.eli5: Skipping the front desk when you move rooms is quick, but the new room might give you a key to the wrong floor. The rule is: if the shortcut would give you the wrong access, make it fail and go back to the desk.

sections.title: Security Analysis
sections.content:
The threat model assumes an attacker who sees all traffic, can alter, forge, replay and reroute messages, can be a principal or an outsider, and can compromise any sufficiently old key. Threats include stolen peers or authenticators, downgrade attacks, spoofing, disclosure of keying material, stale keys, privilege elevation, man-in-the-middle attacks, authenticator fraud and denial of service.

The analysis then checks EAP methods, AAA protocols and Secure Association Protocols against the requirements of RFC 4962: preventing the domino effect, cryptographic algorithm independence, authenticating all parties, replay protection, strong and fresh session keys, limited key scope, uniquely named keys and authorization.

Several findings stand out. RADIUS without IPsec cannot negotiate its integrity algorithm and relies on MD5. A compromised pass-through authenticator can give the peer misleading information, which is why channel binding is needed to check lower-layer parameters. The IEEE 802.11 4-way handshake protects every message except the first, and proof of possession does not prove authorization. Caching creates denial-of-service risk, so servers and authenticators can limit the persistent state kept per peer.
sections.eli5: The authors imagine a very sneaky attacker and then check every part of the system, one lock at a time, against a list of good practices. They note where a lock is weak, such as an old kind of fingerprint check.

items.title: Mode independence
items.text: Methods work the same whether or not the authenticator passes traffic through to a backend server.

items.title: Media independence
items.text: Methods do not depend on the lower layer they run over.

items.title: Method independence
items.text: A pass-through authenticator does not need to implement the methods it forwards.

items.title: Ciphersuite independence
items.text: Exported keys work with any ciphersuite negotiated in the lower layer.
